slides.label: Extrinsic Constructions
slides.notes: Open with the chapter question: before the course defines parallel transport intrinsically, it builds a practical outside-in rule. The ambient space lets us move an arrow, but the surface only accepts tangent arrows, so the first model of transport is a repeated act of projection back into the tangent plane.

slides.label: The Projection Rule
slides.notes: The key construction is a split of an ordinary ambient derivative into tangent and normal parts. The covariant derivative is the tangent projection of the ambient rate of change. If that projected part is zero, the vector is parallel along the curve according to this extrinsic model.

slides.label: Discrete Transport Around A Loop
slides.notes: Use the local artifact to make the algorithm concrete. Move a tangent vector a short step in the surrounding space, project it into the next tangent plane, renormalize if desired, and repeat. Around a closed loop the returned direction can disagree with the starting direction, and that mismatch is a probe for curvature.

slides.label: Where Projection Happens
slides.notes: The surface plot emphasizes that projection is not a drawing trick. Each point has its own tangent plane and normal, so the vector must be judged against the tangent space at the point where it lands. The ambient coordinates are convenient bookkeeping, but the accepted component is the tangent one.

slides.label: Geodesics As Self-Parallel Tangents
slides.notes: A geodesic is the special case where the curve's own tangent vector survives this test. Its ambient acceleration may point away from the surface, but the tangent component of the acceleration vanishes. That is why a geodesic is straight from the surface's point of view even when it visibly bends in space.

slides.label: Parallel Transport Along Geodesics
slides.notes: Once the tangent of a geodesic is self-parallel, it becomes a calibration path for other transported vectors. The lesson is not that geodesics make transport trivial, but that the along-path comparison rule can be stated without referring to sideways turning inside the surface.

slides.label: Potato-Peeler Development
slides.notes: The potato-peeler model makes the same idea tactile. A narrow strip is peeled from the surface and flattened; along a geodesic the strip develops without sideways correction. The metric coefficients tell us how coordinate steps become lengths, so the flattened strip is not a freehand sketch but a measurement device.

slides.label: Representation Versus Invariant
slides.notes: This chapter is a warning against mistaking the scaffold for the geometry. Coordinates, embeddings, and frame drawings can all change. What survives are metric measurements, tangent projections, and comparison results such as a loop's returned angle. The extrinsic construction is useful exactly because it shows what must later be defined intrinsically.

slides.label: Recap And Outlook
slides.notes: Close by naming the bridge built in the chapter. Ambient projection gives a first workable transport rule; geodesics appear as curves with self-parallel tangents; the peeled-strip model turns the rule into a physical development. The next intrinsic formulation should feel less mysterious because every term already has a visible job.
